text: Research paths / Reading list From two phases to chemistry and cloud formation. FGH established a two-phase picture. Later work changed the heating and chemical inputs, then followed fronts, turbulence, and magnetized clouds. This reading list connects those questions to the calculations we can document and explore. Listed references are not completed reproductions. Bibliography and abstracts have been checked; equations, target figures, and data availability need individual review. This page groups papers by research path; each path runs from oldest to newest. For one chronological list across all paths, open all papers by year. Publication years are used where confirmed, with preprint dates noted separately. Scope for modern simulations Choose the scientific question before the computing budget. Reproducing a large multidimensional simulation can require substantial computing time, storage, and access to original inputs. Our modern-paper exhibits can instead provide a source guide, documented setup, analysis of available outputs, or a small benchmark that isolates a physical mechanism. Source and method: link the paper and any public code, inputs, and datasets; record what is actually available. Reuse and analysis: regenerate a diagnostic from released outputs where possible, preserving units, provenance, and processing steps. Small calculations: evaluate an analytic relation, a one-zone chemical model, a front, or a convergence test within an explicit reduced scope. Optional full runs: record the resolution, solver, hardware, wall time, and storage needed. A full 2D/3D rerun is not a condition for completing a source or analysis exhibit. For new nonlinear thermal-instability simulation exhibits, the thermal-conduction treatment and resolution of its relevant scales are selection criteria to audit explicitly. Analytical theory and microphysical rate references are documented separately. Digitized published curves will be identified as digitizations. Reduced models will state their omissions; their results will not be labeled as full-simulation reproductions. Reading path Foundations: thermal stability, buoyancy and conductive phase exchange Parker (1953) provides a pre-Field historical starting point. Chandrasekhar (1961) supplies the buoyancy-driven convection and Boussinesq comparison. Balbus (1986) extends the local stability analysis to evolving backgrounds, while Begelman & McKee (1990) treats conductive mass exchange between phases. Analytical background references and conduction-resolved simulation exhibits have different roles. 1953 / Reference listed Instability of Thermal Fields Eugene N. Parker ApJ 117, 431 Thermal-field stability before Field (1965), with a solar-atmosphere application. Proposed scope: Historical background: compare the temperature-field equation, conduction, and heating assumptions with Field’s hydrodynamic analysis. Keep the original solar application distinct from neutral interstellar gas. Source & bibliography ↗ 1961 / Reference listed Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Stability S. Chandrasekhar Monograph: Clarendon Press, Oxford (1961); later Dover edition, ISBN 9780486640716 Buoyancy-driven thermal convection and its Boussinesq approximation: a fluid-dynamical comparison with radiative thermal instability. Proposed scope: Proposed entry point: the onset of convection in a layer heated from below, followed by a neutral Rayleigh curve for explicitly specified mechanical and thermal boundaries. Retain velocity, perturbation pressure and buoyancy; distinguish this mechanism from the Field radiative-condensation mode. No equation or figure reproduction yet. Source & bibliography ↗ 1972 / Computed prototype / technical review pending Formation of Clouds in a Cooling Interstellar Medium Schwarz, McCray & Stein ApJ175,673–686 Thermal conduction and recombination shape perturbations growing in an isochorically cooling background. Proposed scope: Early-time linear Figure2 plus a nonlinear3pc/10percent Lagrangian prototype without a Riemann solver. Historical-scale64/96/128-cell runs and a512-cell auxiliary comparison document conservation, timing/input differences, and unresolved conductive-front resolution. Source & bibliography ↗Cooling-medium condensation: Figure2 prototype →Nonlinear Lagrangian condensation → 1986 / Reference listed Local Dynamic Thermal Instability Steven A. Balbus ApJ Letters 303, L79–L82 Local thermal-instability criteria for time-dependent background flows; transport processes are omitted in this analytical treatment. Proposed scope: Compare the loss-per-unit-mass convention and the derivative of loss/T with Field’s equilibrium criterion. This is analytical background, not a conduction-resolved nonlinear simulation exhibit. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1990 / Reference listed Global Effects of Thermal Conduction on Two-Phase Media Begelman & McKee ApJ 358, 375–391 Thermal conduction transfers mass between phases through evaporation and condensation; a Field-length scale organizes the competition with heating and cooling. Proposed scope: Audit the Field-length definition and the assumptions of classical conduction, uniform pressure, and small cloud filling factor. Compare reduced evolution equations while retaining the original thermal model and application. Source & bibliography ↗ Convection and radiative condensation are distinct: Chandrasekhar’s textbook is included as a foundational monograph, not a journal paper. Its proposed benchmark is buoyancy-driven convection of a layer heated from below. Rayleigh-number onset must not be identified with the cooling-derivative criterion for the Field condensation mode, which does not require gravity. The Boussinesq comparison retains velocity, a pressure constraint and buoyancy while filtering acoustic compressibility. It does not mean zero flow or zero pressure gradient. The resulting hierarchy for the proposed explanation is: selected reaction–diffusion models → Boussinesq fluid dynamics → compressible thermal gas. These are different approximations and drivers, not a single universal equation. Spiegel & Veronis (1960), On the Boussinesq Approximation for a Compressible Fluid, gives a primary-source account of its assumptions: a thin layer relative to scale heights and suitably small fluctuations. Density variations remain in the buoyancy force. The compressible-fluid reduction also requires care with the adiabatic temperature gradient. The textbook’s bibliography is checked; its exact equations, sections and figures are not yet audited because full-text access attempts failed. No textbook figure is claimed reproduced. Source review and proposed scope / JSON. Reading path Rate and ionization lineage: atomic data, grains and charge balance A separate branch follows the atomic and molecular data, radiative yields, and heating/cooling prescriptions behind gas models. Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) extends the path to grain-size-dependent charge equilibrium in shielded molecular gas. These papers are not all chemical-network rate catalogs. 1960 / Source rates audited / truncated model Cooling of the Interstellar Clouds in Region of Neutral Hydrogen Takayanagi & Nishimura PASJ 12, 77–105 H₂ rotational excitation and the cooling budget of neutral clouds. Proposed scope: 34 printed upward H + para-H2 rates audited on p. 82; a truncated steady level calculation is compared with 60 printed cooling values. Twelve numerical checks pass, while the largest Table 2 discrepancy is retained at about 21.72%. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗H₂ rates & cooling comparison → 1961 / Reference listed Radiations from the Interstellar Hydrogen Atoms Hayakawa, Nishimura & Takayanagi PASJ 13, 184–206 Excitation and ionization of interstellar hydrogen by suprathermal particles, connecting radiation and cloud heating. Proposed scope: Audit particle spectra, excitation/ionization definitions, and radiation/heating yields separately from thermally averaged chemical rates. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1968 / Reference listed Heating of H I Regions by Energetic Particles Spitzer & Tomasko ApJ 152, 971 Energetic-particle heating and ionization of H I, including secondary-electron energy deposition and metal cooling. Proposed scope: Prioritize the definitions of primary/total ionization rates and energy per ionization when comparing with FGH/GHF. Audit secondary-electron treatment, abundances, and collider channels before implementing a heating benchmark. Source & bibliography ↗ 1969 / Reference listed Thermal and Dynamical Evolution of Gas Clouds of Various Masses Hattori, Nakano & Hayashi Progress of Theoretical Physics 42, 781–798 Gas-cloud evolution with molecular/atomic line cooling, grains, radiation, and ionization in transparent and opaque regimes. Proposed scope: Inventory the individual heating/cooling prescriptions and their cited atomic/molecular data before choosing a small thermal-evolution calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1972 / Reference listed Heating and Ionization of HI Regions Dalgarno & McCray ARA&A 10, 375–426 A historical review of heating and ionization processes in neutral interstellar gas. Proposed scope: Use as a source map for historical heating/cooling processes. Audit individual formulas, ionization fractions, abundance assumptions, and original rate references before selecting a cooling-curve calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1991 / Reference listed Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi ApJ 368, 181–194 Ionization–recombination equilibrium with electrons, ions and charged grains; grain-size distributions affect magnetic coupling in shielded molecular clouds. Proposed scope: Candidate: Figure1 charged-species abundances at10K for the standard MRN grain distribution, before comparing the other grain models. Recover the required reaction rates and PaperI inputs first. This is a charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-equilibrium curve or a reproduced magnetic-flux-loss calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Field et al. (1968) discusses Takayanagi and Nishimura’s H₂ excitation data. FGH (1969) cites Hayakawa, Nishimura and Takayanagi’s cosmic-ray heating work. Hattori, Nakano and Hayashi’s reference list includes both papers. These links identify a route for source tracing; they do not establish that later models use identical coefficients. For each future rate record, we will distinguish cross sections, rate coefficients, energy-loss coefficients, volumetric rates, and yields. Species, colliders, units, normalization, validity range, population assumptions, source equation/table, and correction/code version will accompany the numerical formula. The Takayanagi–Nishimura rate audit now transcribes 34 coefficients and tests a finite level model. Its Table 2 mismatches remain visible. Other coefficient sets still require equation/table review; the citation links alone do not validate them. Lineage evidence and proposed coefficient-record fields / JSON Ionization fraction is a separate branch: Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) calculates electron, ion and charged-grain abundances before magnetic coupling. Figures1–4 compare grain distributions. Figure1 is a possible small charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-balance calculation. Its axes use abundances relative to total hydrogen nuclei and nH/ζ, with ζ the ionization rate per hydrogen molecule; these conventions must not be silently interchanged with FGH’s atomic-gas definitions. The paper calls Umebayashi & Nakano (1990), Magnetic flux loss from interstellar clouds, MNRAS243,103–113, PaperI and builds on its reaction scheme. The publisher’s abstract confirms an ionization–recombination equilibrium calculation; its full rate-table audit remains pending. Distinguish the ionization rate ζ from the resulting electron fraction, and distinguish both from a cooling coefficient. Source review and parameter conventions / JSON. Reading path Heating, cooling, and public chemistry Cosmic-ray heating in FGH, grain photoelectric heating in Bakes & Tielens (1994), Wolfire (1995, 2003), and GOW (2017) provide a path to public chemistry implementations. These models use different physical assumptions; they are not interchangeable cooling prescriptions. 1994 / Reference listed The Photoelectric Heating Mechanism for Very Small Graphitic Grains and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons Bakes & Tielens ApJ 427 (1994) Photoelectric heating by small carbonaceous grains and PAHs, including grain charging and a heating-efficiency prescription. Proposed scope: Trace the photoelectric-heating input used in later neutral-gas models. Audit radiation-field normalization, electron density, grain population, temperature range, and net gas–grain energy exchange before plotting the efficiency fit. Source & bibliography ↗ 1995 / Reference listed The Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium Wolfire, Hollenbach, McKee, Tielens & Bakes ApJ 443, 152–168 Photoelectric heating by small grains and PAHs, X-ray/cosmic-ray ionization, and atomic phase equilibrium. Proposed scope: Audit the heating/cooling terms and identify a local equilibrium curve for a modest-cost calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2003 / Reference listed Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium in the Galaxy Wolfire, McKee, Hollenbach & Tielens ApJ 587, 278–311 Revised atomic-gas microphysics and the allowed two-phase pressure range across the Galactic disk. Proposed scope: Compare physical inputs with the 1995 model before attempting an equilibrium calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2017 / Reference listed A Simple and Accurate Network for Hydrogen and Carbon Chemistry in the Interstellar Medium Gong, Ostriker & Wolfire ApJ 843, 38 A compact chemical network with an author-maintained public PDR implementation and rate corrections. Proposed scope: Pin a corrected rate/code version, inspect units and validity ranges, then choose a small chemical or thermal benchmark. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2023 / Reference listed Implementation of Chemistry in the Athena++ Code Gong, Ho, Stone, Ostriker, Caselli, Grassi, C.-G. Kim, J.-G. Kim & Halevi ApJS 268, 42 A public chemistry framework including GOW17, general KIDA networks, and coupled thermal/chemical evolution. Proposed scope: Begin with published tests, public inputs, or a small one-zone/1D case; full 3D runs are optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Reading path Phase-transition fronts: from planar balance to curved clouds Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner (1969) and Penston–Brown (1970) connect to Elphick–Regev–Shaviv (1992), Ferrara–Shchekinov (1993), Shchekinov–Ibáñez (2001), Nagashima and collaborators’ curved-front work, and Kim & Kim’s (2013) conductive evaporation-front instability. Static balance, steady mass flux, perturbations, and spherical survival times are distinct computational questions. 1969 / Reference listed The Phase Equilibrium and Dynamics of a Gas Volume That Is Heated and Cooled Zel’dovich & Pikel’ner Soviet Physics JETP 29, 170–173; Russian original: ZhETF 56, 310–315 Conductive interfaces select the stationary two-phase pressure; away from that pressure the boundary moves. Proposed scope: Candidate: the planar saturation condition and a steady front or front-speed calculation. Specify the heat-loss law, conductivity, signs, and boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗ 1970 / Reference listed The Cloud–Intercloud Phase-Change in the Interstellar Medium Penston & Brown MNRAS 150, 373–388 Thermal balance across a conducting cloud–intercloud interface adds a condition beyond pressure balance. Proposed scope: Candidate: compare the stationary interface criterion and thermal timescales with the Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner formulation before choosing a small front calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1992 / Reference listed Dynamics of Fronts in Thermally Bistable Fluids Elphick, Regev & Shaviv ApJ 392, 106–117 Isobaric conductive fronts, a Lyapunov functional, equal-depth potential minima and interacting cloud boundaries. Proposed scope: The source equations are reviewed; no numerical reproduction yet. Candidate: the cubic benchmark, static kink or front speed versus potential-depth difference, retaining the Lagrangian mass coordinate and state-dependent mobility. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1993 / Reference listed Dynamics of Conductive/Cooling Fronts: Cloud Implosion and Thermal Solitons Ferrara & Shchekinov ApJ 417, 595 Conductive and radiative interfaces admit static and steady fronts, cloud compression, and soliton-like solutions. Proposed scope: Start with planar static/steady front equations, boundary heat fluxes, and the mechanical analogy. Select a small ODE benchmark after auditing the heat-loss law, conductivity, and pressure/flow assumptions. Cloud implosion simulations are a separate, optional scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2001 / Reference listed Interaction of Small Planar Perturbations with Cooling-Conductive Fronts Shchekinov & Ibáñez ApJ 563, 209–220 Acoustic and entropy perturbations interact with steady subsonic cold–hot fronts in one-dimensional planar geometry, with heating, cooling, and thermal conduction. Proposed scope: First audit the steady planar background and its mass-flux eigenvalue at prescribed pressure, as discussed by Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), section 3. Then consider reflection/transmission coefficients as a separate perturbation benchmark. Do not equate this one-dimensional perturbation problem with transverse front corrugation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2005 / Reference listed Evaporation and condensation of H I clouds in thermally bistable interstellar media: semi-analytic description of isobaric dynamics of curved interfaces Nagashima, Koyama & Inutsuka MNRAS Letters 361, L25–L29 Curvature modifies evaporation and condensation for cylindrical, spherical, and general fronts under an isobaric approximation. Proposed scope: Candidate: evaluate the semi-analytic curvature correction and compare planar, cylindrical, and spherical limits using a small ODE calculation. Keep the polynomial heat-loss model distinct from later realistic fits. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed How Long Can Tiny H I Clouds Survive? Nagashima, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ Letters 652, L41–L44 Spherical cloud evaporation times depend on cloud size and ambient pressure, with a quasi-steady interpretation. Proposed scope: Candidate: reproduce the analytic timescale/critical-radius relation and, if practical, a one-dimensional radial benchmark. Large multidimensional reruns are unnecessary for this scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed Nonlinear Development of Thermal Instability without External Forcing Koyama & Inutsuka arXiv:astro-ph/0605528 (2006 preprint; journal publication not verified) Conduction, viscosity, and cloud motions in multidimensional nonlinear thermal instability without external forcing. Proposed scope: Start with the preprint’s physical mechanism, diagnostics, and any available outputs. A full 2D/3D rerun is optional; its journal-publication status remains unverified. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2013 / Reference listed Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium Jeong-Gyu Kim & Woong-Tae Kim ApJ 779, 48 Thermal conduction suppresses short-wavelength corrugations of CNM–WNM evaporation fronts. Linear stability analysis connects to nonlinear front deformation and enhanced evaporation. Proposed scope: Detailed reconstruction of AppendixA with coupled eigenfunctions as the required output. Primary target: Figure9 temperature and transverse-velocity profiles from the same normalized mode; supporting targets are the background front, Figure5 dispersion and long-wave/cutoff limits. Source-audited plan only; no Kim eigenfunctions computed yet. Nonlinear2D remains separate and optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Gradient-flow connection: Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) gives an isobaric reduction in Lagrangian mass coordinates, a Lyapunov functional, equal-minima ZP fronts and front interactions. The biophysical comparisons follow wave-pinning, conserved protein redistribution and neural excitability, with their distinct conservation laws and scope. Conductive front instability: Kim & Kim (2013) explicitly includes thermal conduction in the linear stability analysis and nonlinear evolution of evaporation fronts. This provides a comparison with Inoue et al. (2006), while Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) supplies a related steady-front classification. A stability spectrum, a steady-solution classification, and nonlinear saturation are different reproduction targets. The user requires detailed coupled eigenfunctions, especially Figure9, as the Kim2013 reconstruction target; a dispersion curve alone will not complete that task. Steady flow and perturbations: Ferrara & Shchekinov (1993) studies static/steady front properties and their dynamical evolution. Shchekinov & Ibáñez (2001) studies planar acoustic/entropy perturbations interacting with steady subsonic fronts. In section 3, Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) explicitly describes the latter work as determining the ZP mass flux j(P) through an eigenvalue problem. We will audit the steady background before attempting perturbation coefficients. This citation does not establish identical cooling laws or numerical parameters. Related entries: Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama (2006) addresses front stability; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) studies dynamical condensation fronts; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2014) studies interfacial energy transfer in a bistable medium. The Field-condition paper provides a connection to conduction and resolution. Different heat-loss laws, geometries, and dynamical approximations must be preserved when comparing these studies. A reading path is not proof of identical assumptions or coefficients. Reading path Hennebelle, Burkert, and collaborators: condensation and fragmentation Converging flows connect thermal bistability to cloud formation. Hennebelle and collaborators examine dynamical condensation, magnetic fields, and turbulent two-phase gas; Burkert and collaborators examine cooling perturbations, colliding flows, and fragmentation. These are related research paths, not a claim that the listed papers share the same authors or physical model. 1999 / Reference listed Dynamical condensation in a thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Hennebelle & Pérault A&A 351, 309–322 Transonic converging warm flows produce cold condensations; self-similar non-isobaric solutions describe early condensation. Proposed scope: Audit the self-similar solution and size/velocity thresholds versus ambient pressure. Start with analytic relations or a planar one-dimensional benchmark; preserve the original heating/cooling and boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗ 2000 / Reference listed Dynamical condensation in a magnetized and thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Hennebelle & Pérault A&A 359, 1124–1138 Oblique magnetic fields and tension alter condensation in slab geometry; transverse motions can align fields or flows and permit compression. Proposed scope: Compare nonmagnetic, transverse-field, and oblique-field limits using the published self-similar analysis and a small one-dimensional MHD benchmark. Audit the angle and field-strength assumptions before choosing a figure. Source & bibliography ↗ 2000 / Reference listed Thermal Instability and the Formation of Clumpy Gas Clouds Burkert & Lin ApJ 537, 270–282 During radiative cooling, the transition from isobaric to isochoric evolution limits perturbation growth and influences the characteristic clump scale; conduction suppresses small scales. Proposed scope: Audit the growth, transition-temperature, and nonlinear-amplitude estimates. Use small analytic or time-dependent perturbation calculations before considering fragmentation simulations; distinguish cooling backgrounds from thermal equilibrium. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2005 / Reference listed Thermal condensation in a turbulent atomic hydrogen flow Audit & Hennebelle A&A 433, 1–13 Two-dimensional turbulent converging flows condense warm H I into cold structures; the thermally unstable gas fraction correlates with turbulence. Proposed scope: Start with the semi-analytical model for unstable gas and its relation to turbulence. Reanalyse published diagnostics or available outputs after a provenance audit. A full high-resolution two-dimensional run is optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed The Birth of Molecular Clouds: Formation of Atomic Precursors in Colliding Flows Heitsch, Slyz, Devriendt, Hartmann & Burkert ApJ 648, 1052–1065 Colliding atomic flows develop structure through dynamical and thermal instabilities before molecular hydrogen begins to form. Proposed scope: Document the inflow, cooling law, geometry, and instability diagnostics. Prefer reanalysis of available density/temperature and fragmentation outputs; do not require a full multidimensional rerun or imply that this model follows the molecular stage. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2007 / Reference listed On the structure of the turbulent interstellar atomic hydrogen. I. Physical characteristics. Influence and nature of turbulence in a thermally bistable flow Hennebelle & Audit A&A 465, 431–443 High-resolution two-dimensional bistable turbulence produces small-scale CNM structures, a cloud mass spectrum, and distinct density and velocity statistics. Proposed scope: Begin with the analytical mass-spectrum argument and definitions of the measured spectra. Recompute diagnostics only from accessible, documented outputs; retain the dimensionality dependence and avoid treating a small run as a reproduction of the full statistics. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2008 / Reference listed Fragmentation of Shocked Flows: Gravity, Turbulence, and Cooling Heitsch, Hartmann & Burkert ApJ 683, 786–795 Comparing dynamical, thermal, and gravitational timescales identifies where shocked flows fragment and seed local collapse. Proposed scope: A timescale/regime diagram is a promising inexpensive reproduction target. First audit the cooling law, perturbation scales, background state, and boundaries; keep this calculation distinct from a full flow-driven cloud simulation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Publication years determine the order: Audit & Hennebelle (2005) has a 2004 preprint, and Hennebelle & Audit (2007) has a 2006 preprint. For modest computing budgets, the self-similar, perturbation-growth, semi-analytical, and timescale arguments offer entry points. High-resolution multidimensional statistics require suitable released outputs or a separately documented computing plan. Reading path Inoue: fronts, two-fluid gas, and magnetic fields A path from the stability of phase-transition fronts to converging flows and turbulent molecular clouds. 2006 / Reference listed Structure and Stability of Phase Transition Layers in the Interstellar Medium Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ 652, 1331–1338 CNM/WNM fronts, evaporation and condensation, and corrugational stability. Proposed scope: Candidate: a plane-parallel front or the linear growth relation, after checking boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2007 / Reference listed The Role of Ambipolar Diffusion in the Formation Process of Moderately Magnetized Diffuse Clouds Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ 658, L99–L102 Two-fluid condensation and the competition between magnetic flux accumulation and ambipolar diffusion. Proposed scope: Candidate: the analytic field-strength estimate or a small 1D verification case. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2008 / Reference listed Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. I: Methodology and Basic Results Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 687, 303–310 Two-fluid coupling and magnetic limits on condensation in converging atomic flows. Proposed scope: Document the method and inputs; consider a coupling benchmark or analysis of available outputs rather than a full 2D rerun. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2009 / Reference listed Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. II: Are Molecular Clouds Generated Directly from a Warm Neutral Medium? Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 704, 161–169 The angle between inflow and mean magnetic field affects shocked atomic gas and cloud formation. Proposed scope: Compare model assumptions and published diagnostics; reanalyse public outputs if available. Large runs are outside the initial scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2012 / Reference listed Formation of Turbulent and Magnetized Molecular Clouds via Accretion Flows of H I Clouds Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 759, 35 Three-dimensional MHD with chemistry, conduction, and accretion of inhomogeneous atomic gas. Proposed scope: Focus on setup documentation, analysis methods, and any available snapshots. Do not require rerunning the full 3D calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Reading path Iwasaki: condensation, interfaces, and cloud formation Similarity solutions and front structure offer modest-cost entry points. Later multidimensional calculations can be explored through their diagnostics and available data. 2008 / Reference listed Self-similar solutions for the dynamical condensation of a radiative gas layer Iwasaki & Tsuribe MNRAS 387, 1554–1562 Non-equilibrium thermal condensation described by a family of plane-parallel similarity solutions. Proposed scope: Candidate: similarity profiles and limiting scalings, using an ODE solver and a small 1D comparison. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2009 / Reference listed Fragmentation of a dynamically condensing radiative layer Iwasaki & Tsuribe A&A 508, 725–735 Perturbation growth on a time-dependent, dynamically condensing background. Proposed scope: Candidate: linear perturbation evolution on the time-dependent similarity solution, before a full nonlinear calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2012 / Computed prototype / technical review pending Structure of dynamical condensation fronts in the interstellar medium Iwasaki & Inutsuka MNRAS 423, 3638–3645 Condensation-front families parameterized by pressure and mass flux, with cooling- and Field-length regimes. Proposed scope: Confirmed target: Figures 5 and 7, pressure–mass-flux classification. A computed prototype reproduces nine stated example classes and passes 30 checks. Unavailable CNM branches and temperature-limited cells are masked; the jcrit overlay and complete boundary comparison await technical review. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗Figures 5 & 7: computed prototype → 2014 / Reference listed Self-Sustained Turbulence without Dynamical Forcing: A Two-Dimensional Study of a Bistable Interstellar Medium Iwasaki & Inutsuka ApJ 784, 115 Thermal conduction, phase transitions, viscosity, and kinetic-energy transfer in a bistable medium. Proposed scope: Prioritize published energy budgets and analysis of available outputs. A small front problem can isolate the mechanism without reproducing the full 2D run. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2019 / Reference listed The Early Stage of Molecular Cloud Formation by Compression of Two-phase Atomic Gases Iwasaki, Tomida, Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 873, 6; preprint first posted in 2018 Three-dimensional MHD, non-equilibrium chemistry, and the critical magnetic-field/inflow angle for cloud formation. Proposed scope: Candidate: evaluate the analytic critical-angle relation and reanalyse available outputs; full parameter-survey reruns are optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ GOW / Code and rate provenance Follow the corrected rates to their implementation. The GOW paper has a 2018 erratum, and Gong’s code page lists further corrections and updates. The original paper, its erratum, a revised preprint, and an evolving code repository are separate references. Before a benchmark, we will pin the actual implementation and audit its rate definitions and units. We recorded a public PDR-code commit for reference, but have not compiled it or validated its rates. The linked code and documentation remain maintained by their authors. gow17-paper ↗ — First posted in 2016; v4 dated 2019. Published article and later corrections must be tracked separately. gow17-erratum ↗ — Reaction 1 temperature exponent in the printed table is corrected. The authors state their original calculations used the correct formula. gow-author-corrections ↗ — Additional rate updates and a clarification that the CR heating normalization uses the primary rate per H nucleus. This is a live page, not a frozen rate version. gow-pdr-code ↗ — Commit recorded for provenance only. Not built or benchmarked here. Recorded snapshot: 2d903af68145 ↗ athena-chemistry ↗ — Documents GOW17 and a general KIDA interface. No Athena++ code version or network has yet been benchmarked in this archive. Links checked on 3 November 2026. Resource provenance / JSON · Complete paper catalog / JSON Connect these references to the current exhibits. The corrected KI2002 equilibrium benchmark includes stability branches, ZP saturation pressure and all three thermal-equilibrium intersections. Model-specific landmarks retain density conventions and unresolved cases. The Maxwell equal-area historical aside traces the primary publications and distinguishes its integral from ZP selection. The same aside develops a scalar Ginzburg–Landau connection, with Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) as a direct precedent. Field’s stability map connects to front and perturbation problems. FGH/GHF two-phase equilibrium prototype, historical ingredients, and reduced cold branch give a starting point for comparing historical and later microphysics.
